segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Chapter 5. What Was Seen.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The library window looks north up the lane and takes in the corner of the green, and Mrs Hale had been at it since the coach came in, the coach being worth watching. She therefore saw Nye's cart come round with the hurdles still on it. She saw Mr Rowe get down and hand Miss Vane down after him. She saw no maid, no Mrs Pike, and no daylight, and she saw Miss Vane laughing. The whole of it took half a minute. It kept the parish occupied until Tuesday.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By eight the next morning she had told the ostler at the Bell, both the Barrow girls, and a woman from Ropley who had only come in for tape. She told it each time precisely as it had happened, which was what made it so hard afterwards to fix on anybody as the inventor of the rest.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She told Mrs Pike at Mrs Pike's own gate, before nine.

segments.speaker: Mrs Hale
segments.text: Six miles out and six miles back and coming in at dusk, and him handing her down in front of the whole Bell yard, and her laughing so she could not get her foot to the step.

segments.speaker: Mrs Honoria Pike
segments.text: There. There. I said Wednesday would answer. I said it at my own table with the cloth still on it, and there was not one of you would believe me.

segments.speaker: Mrs Hale
segments.text: You did say so.

segments.speaker: Mrs Honoria Pike
segments.text: A fortnight is all it wanted. And her uncle holds the living, which is the beauty of it entirely.

segments.speaker: Mrs Hale
segments.text: Whose uncle?

segments.speaker: Mrs Honoria Pike
segments.text: Miss Marchmont's uncle.

segments.speaker: Mrs Hale
segments.text: It was not Miss Marchmont in the cart. It was Miss Vane.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Mrs Pike went indoors and shut her own door in Mrs Hale's face, which she had never done to anybody in thirty years. She had sent them off herself. She had stood on that step with the note in her hand and told the girl that thread would keep.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Before noon she had assured the sexton, Mrs Yardley, and Hollis's housekeeper that it was nothing at all, nothing whatever, a wheel and a mason and no more in it than that. By four o'clock the parish was entirely satisfied that there was a great deal in it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Judith went up on the Monday for the black thread she had not got on the Friday. The younger Barrow girl was minding the counter, and was kind, and lowered her voice, and said that everyone thought it a shame, and that it must have been dreadful to be seen crying on the curate's arm before all those people at the Bell, and that Sarah Copp said he had spoken there in the road and been refused.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: Where did you have that?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The girl said she had it from her mother, who had it from Mrs Pike, who had said there was nothing in it at all.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: Two reels. And I will take the Cobbe list down off the pin while I am here, since nobody has asked for it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She paid, and went down the stairs, and crossed the green at a pace her brother could hear through the wall of the dispensary. She had been laughed at in this parish before. She had never before been pitied for a thing that had not happened.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Owen had it an hour later from a carter's wife who had come in about a cough and stayed for the rest of it. He weighed out her lozenges, and took her fourpence, and shut the door behind her, and then he untied his apron and hung it on the nail and turned the sign round at half past three in the afternoon, which he had not done on a working day since their father died.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: Owen.

segments.speaker: Mr Owen Vane
segments.text: Get your tea.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: It was a wheel. There is nothing to be done about it that will not make it worse.

segments.speaker: Mr Owen Vane
segments.text: There is one thing, and it is not yours to do, and I have been standing behind that counter all day listening to it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He took his hat down. She stood in the passage with the thread still in her hand and asked him where he was going, though she knew.

segments.speaker: Mr Owen Vane
segments.text: Up to his lodging. I am going to ask him plainly what he means to do about your name, and I shall want an answer before I come home.
